 Will WSU snap 6-game skid vs. Colorado State after FAA travel stoppage? 
 Nov. 13, 2026 at 10:00 pm 
 Listen to article 
 Make us a preferred source 
 By 
 Greg Woods 
 The Spokesman-Review 
 PULLMAN – The night before Washington State was set to host Colorado State, the Rams got a little extra practice in.
 In the chaos of the nationwide flight grounding that swept college football and threatened Saturday’s game between WSU and CSU, set for 7:30 p.m. in Pullman on CBS Sports Network, the Rams found themselves on the tarmac at the Northern Colorado Regional Airport. So they got out and did a walk-through outside the plane.
 If nothing else, it captured the confusion that flooded the country on Friday, when the Federal Aviation Administration ordered all flights to be grounded from early afternoon until around 6 p.m. 
 Looking to earn its first FBS win of the year and end a six-game losing streak, WSU might hope the delays play to its favor. The Cougars (1-8, 0-5 Pac-12) are seeking a win over the Rams (3-6, 1-4), who have lost six of their last seven games and harbor the nation’s worst defense in all kinds of categories.
 In that way, it’s the biggest opportunity of the season for WSU, whose scuffling offense has been to blame for this wayward season. In his fourth career start, Cougar quarterback Owen Eshelman and his offense will look to take down a Colorado State defense that ranks like this nationwide: Last in scoring defense (45 points per game), last in total defense (542 yards per game), second-to-last in third-down conversion defense (54%) and last in yards per play (8).
 Could that be the solution to the Cougars’ ailing offense, which is coming off a bye week? It’s certainly possible, and it might represent WSU’s best chance at an FBS win this fall. After this game, the Cougars will round out the season with a road matchup against Texas State, then a home FLEX game, which will likely bring Oregon State to Pullman for a second clash between the Beavers and Cougars.
 Advertising 
 Those two games don’t profile as clear-cut chances to earn wins. WSU’s home game against Colorado State does — especially considering the travel delays that the Rams faced getting into the area.
 “You can’t let the results dictate your behavior,” WSU defensive tackle Kaden Beatty said at the beginning of the week. “It’s like Coach Moore says: same guy every single day. I love this. I love playing football. I’m on fire for my work every single day. I come in here with a smile, regardless of our record. If we have no wins or we’re winning every single game, I’m gonna be on fire for my work and excited to be in this building.”
 The Cougars could use some of that mentality to take down the Rams, especially considering that starting wide receiver Darrius Clemons is questionable with an ankle injury he suffered last month against Utah State. He has missed the past three games. With 20 catches for 218 yards, his absence has made things even harder on a Cougar offense trying to find its footing.
 What will that look like on Saturday evening? 
 Here’s one possibility worth keeping an eye on: How will the Cougar running backs fare? As the team heads into Week 11, WSU’s trio of Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi are averaging a meager 46 yards on 15 carries in nine games against FBS competition. They haven’t managed any consistency, but that could change against the Rams’ defense, which is permitting an average of 271 yards per game — dead last in the country by nearly 30 yards.
 That could be a boon for the Cougars’ rushing attack, which figured to be one of the team’s top strengths headed into the season, especially considering the time and effort coach Kirby Moore spent luring Vorhees and Pulalasi away from the transfer portal. They haven’t been able to deliver on that, and part of the blame goes to the WSU offensive line, which has often languished in the short-yardage department.
 What’s the solution to those problems? There may not be an obvious long-term fix, but one of the short-term variety could be facing the Rams’ defense, which is averaging 6.8 yards per rush — also last in the country. 
 Advertising 
 Opponents are also averaging nearly 280 rushing yards per game against CSU, which fired previous defensive coordinator Tyson Summers mid-game against Oregon State earlier this year. That hasn’t done much to shore things up for Jim Mora’s team, which gives up about 11.4 yards per pass, another mark that ranks last in the country.
 “It’s just another great opportunity for us to run the ball,” WSU left tackle Ashton Tripp said. “And then, like I said earlier, just getting back to the basics. Break their will and make them quit.”
 Still, WSU shouldn’t view this as an easy win. For as rotten a season as the Rams’ defense has had, their team has some reasons for optimism. Their 10 sacks are better than WSU’s eight. And CSU ranks first in the Pac-12 in forced fumbles (eight) and interceptions (nine). That should be a warning for Eshelman, who threw an interception in his group’s last game, a road defeat to San Diego State on Halloween night.
 Above all, though, WSU needs a win in this game. The Cougars could be looking at a one-win season without it. Can they deliver? Ironically, they may be getting some help from an unexpected source: air traffic delays.
 Greg Woods : Washington State beat writer for The Spokesman-Review
